lesson.title: Peeling Back Every Layer: Solving Multi-Step Equations
lesson.summary: Multi-step equations require extra preparation, distributing and combining like terms, before the familiar two-step process of undoing operations in reverse order can finish the job.
lesson.body:
Multi-step equations look more complicated than one-step or two-step equations, but the extra complexity almost always comes from needing to simplify each side first, not from any genuinely new solving technique. The two most common preparation moves are distributing a number across parentheses, using the distributive property, and combining like terms on the same side of the equation. Once both sides are fully simplified, what remains is typically just a two-step equation, solved the same way already covered.

The distributive property, a(b + c) = ab + ac, is often the very first move needed, since many multi-step equations hide parentheses that must be expanded before terms can be combined. Skipping this step, or distributing incorrectly, is one of the most common sources of error in multi-step equations, so it deserves careful attention before anything else happens.

Work through 3(x + 2) - 4 = 2x + 7. First distribute the 3 across the parentheses: 3(x) + 3(2) - 4 = 2x + 7, which gives 3x + 6 - 4 = 2x + 7. Next, combine like terms on the left side: 6 - 4 = 2, so the equation becomes 3x + 2 = 2x + 7. Now the variable appears on both sides, so the next move is to gather the variable terms onto one side by subtracting 2x from both sides: 3x + 2 - 2x = 2x + 7 - 2x, which simplifies to x + 2 = 7. This is now a one-step equation: subtract 2 from both sides to get x = 5.

Check the solution by substituting x = 5 into the original equation. Left side: 3(5 + 2) - 4 = 3(7) - 4 = 21 - 4 = 17. Right side: 2(5) + 7 = 10 + 7 = 17. Both sides equal 17, confirming x = 5 is correct.

A second example shows both sides needing distribution before anything else can happen. Consider 5(x - 1) = 3(x + 3). Distribute on both sides: 5x - 5 = 3x + 9. Next, gather the variable terms on one side by subtracting 3x from both sides: 5x - 5 - 3x = 3x + 9 - 3x, which simplifies to 2x - 5 = 9. This is now a two-step equation: add 5 to both sides to get 2x = 14, then divide both sides by 2 to get x = 7. Checking, the left side becomes 5(7 - 1) = 5(6) = 30, and the right side becomes 3(7 + 3) = 3(10) = 30. Both sides equal 30, confirming x = 7 is correct.

The overall strategy for any multi-step equation follows a consistent order: distribute any parentheses first, combine like terms on each side separately, then move all variable terms to one side and all constant terms to the other side using addition or subtraction, and finally divide or multiply to isolate the variable completely, exactly as in a two-step equation. Every skill used here, the distributive property, combining like terms, and the reverse-order undoing of operations from two-step equations, comes together in this single method, which is why building each earlier skill solidly matters so much before tackling equations that combine all of them at once.
